This state/province sits squarely in the country's geography where traditional-court jurisdiction is most extensive, following the map of territories that formerly held separate nominal status: an international rights organisation's analysis of the country's 2019 traditional-leadership act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose customary adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law - with a consent presumption running against the individual - is the principal sub-national legal divergence in the country. The act was declared invalid by the constitutional court in 2023 in a town located in this state/province, but the ruling was suspended and the replacement bill has been delayed. No religious criminal law exists in this state/province; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

This state/province is also, apart from the three most urbanised states/provinces, the only one to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010); the national campaign review that catalogues them records that only three such quantitative studies have ever been attempted countrywide - giving this state/province a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here have historically been more likely to surface in research than in the unreported "dark figure" that characterises most of the country. No trans-specific incident series was found; the 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people, and its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy setting.
